questions.q: You need a row for every missing day between a store's first and last date. Which is the right design?
options: One date range for all stores
A date range built per store from its own min and max
why: That adds days before a store opened.
Correct: each store has its own span.
Sorting adds no rows.
Dropping duplicates removes rows.

questions.q: Which merge_asof setting avoids look-ahead leakage?
why: Nearest may take a later reading.
Forward takes later readings.
Correct: backward takes only earlier or equal times.
That setting only removes equal times; it does not fix direction.

questions.q: Scenario: sensor A has a reading at 12:00:00. Sensor B has readings at 11:59:10 and 12:00:20. tolerance = 60 s, direction backward. Which B reading is matched?
why: Correct: it is the latest earlier reading, 50 seconds old (within 60).
12:00:20 is after 12:00:00, so it is the future.
Only one row is matched.
The 11:59:10 reading is within tolerance, so there is a match.

questions.q: Values: [3, 4, 4, 9, 10, 10, 11, 30], tol = 1. What is the length of the longest calm stretch?
questions.why: Run 9, 10, 10, 11 has changes 1, 0, 1, all at most 1. Its length is 4. The run 3, 4, 4 has length 3.

questions.q: Why is looping over every row of a 100,000-row DataFrame a bad idea in an OA?
options: It is slow and often hits the time limit; group operations are faster
why: It is allowed, just slow.
Correct: vectorized or group operations run much faster.
Looping does not by itself change the index.
It does not sort.

questions.q: Scenario: hidden tests fail with 'incompatible merge keys' on an empty second table. What is the likely cause?
options: The empty table has a different column type (dtype) than the other
why: Tolerance does not cause key type errors.
Correct: an empty frame can default to a different dtype, and the key types must match.
A version issue is less likely than a dtype mismatch.
Sorting does not cause a type error.
